open_points.subject: OwnerFormField and its vocabularies
open_points.text: The models M01–M28 as the domain's vocabulary — among them the forms of a pointer's publisher and an audit entry's subject (M13–M19), the owner session's pending confirmation and uploaded file (M20, M21) and the row shapes of the data provider's seven tables (M22–M28)
open_points.question: Which module owns M29 OwnerFormField and the OwnerFormCarrier and FormValueKind vocabularies now used by data_provider and owner_interface?
options: Extend models to own M01–M29 and all eight table-row models plus both enumerations
Make data_provider own the row type and enumerations as well as the rows
Split ownership between models and data_provider
open_points.default_guess: Extend models to own OwnerFormField, OwnerFormCarrier and FormValueKind, while data_provider owns only OWNER_FORM_FIELDS and its scalar encoding constants.

witness.initial: State 6 must declare the types and imports for the new owner-form table.
events: The model generator reads the models module responsibility.
It finds that models owns only M01–M28 and seven table row shapes, while data_provider and owner_interface name M29 and its enumerations.
outcomes: The generator adds OwnerFormField and both enumerations to models because they are model vocabulary.
The generator treats them as data_provider-owned release types or leaves them without an owner.
witness.observer: Later generators see different provider modules and dependency graphs.

open_points.subject: OwnerFormCarrier
open_points.text: `OwnerFormCarrier` and `FormValueKind`, by whose members it reads a form field's row
open_points.question: What are the exact members and serialized values of OwnerFormCarrier, and which member denotes OwnerRequest versus OwnerValues?
options: Members OWNER_REQUEST and OWNER_VALUES with explicitly fixed values
Members REQUEST and VALUES with explicitly fixed values
Use model names directly instead of an enumeration
open_points.default_guess: Define OWNER_REQUEST and OWNER_VALUES with stable lowercase serialized values.

witness.initial: OWNER_FORM_FIELDS contains a row for a submitted field.
events: owner_interface reads the row's carrier.
The row must select whether the parsed value is placed in OwnerRequest or OwnerValues.
outcomes: One implementation matches OwnerFormCarrier.OWNER_REQUEST.
Another matches OwnerFormCarrier.REQUEST or compares a string such as "request".
witness.observer: The owner sees the same form populate different parts of the operation request or fail at runtime.

open_points.subject: FormValueKind
open_points.text: how its text is read: as text, as an integer, as true or false, or as an enumeration member's value
open_points.question: What are the exact FormValueKind members and values for the four stated conversions?
options: TEXT, INTEGER, BOOLEAN and ENUM with explicitly fixed values
STRING, INT, BOOL and ENUM_VALUE with explicitly fixed values
Store converter identifiers rather than an enumeration
open_points.default_guess: Define TEXT, INTEGER, BOOLEAN and ENUM with stable lowercase values.

witness.initial: The release contains an OWNER_FORM_FIELDS row whose value kind denotes an integer.
events: data_provider constructs the row.
owner_interface dispatches on the row's FormValueKind member.
outcomes: Both modules use INTEGER and the value is parsed.
One module emits INT while the other expects INTEGER, so the row cannot be handled.
witness.observer: The owner sees a valid submitted numeric field rejected or ignored.

open_points.subject: OwnerFormField destination path
open_points.text:
The row gives the field's name, its path in the owner request or its values, with a tuple's position marked; which of the two it fills; and how its text is read: as text, as an integer, as true or false, or as an enumeration member's value.

Facts: the field's name; what it fills; how its text is read.
open_points.question: Is the full destination path, including every attribute/key segment and tuple position, a distinct fact of OwnerFormField, or is it included in the vague fact “what it fills”; what is its exact type and grammar?
options: Declare carrier and destination path as separate typed facts
Define “what it fills” as one structured destination containing carrier and path
Use a closed destination enumeration rather than paths
open_points.default_guess: Declare separate carrier and structured path facts, with path segments typed explicitly.

witness.initial: Two submitted fields both fill OwnerValues and are both read as text, but one targets a project name and the other a room name.
events: owner_interface looks up each field's OwnerFormField row.
It must navigate from the carrier to the intended destination.
outcomes: The rows carry distinct structured paths and populate the intended fields.
The implementation treats “what it fills” as only the carrier and must hard-code or guess destinations from field names.
witness.observer: operations receives different OwnerValues from the same form.

open_points.subject: OWNER_FORM_POSITION_MARK
open_points.text: its path in the owner request or its values, with a tuple's position marked
open_points.question: What exactly does OWNER_FORM_POSITION_MARK mark, what is its type, where may it appear in a path, how is a tuple index represented, and how are literal path values that resemble the mark distinguished?
options: A sentinel object followed by an integer tuple index
A reserved string segment plus an integer index
A dedicated typed TuplePosition path segment, eliminating the scalar marker
open_points.default_guess: Use a dedicated typed TuplePosition path segment; if the constant must remain, define it as an unambiguous sentinel with a fixed path grammar.

witness.initial: A form field targets the second element of a tuple nested in OwnerValues.
events: The row encodes the destination using OWNER_FORM_POSITION_MARK.
owner_interface walks the encoded path.
outcomes: The marker means that the following segment is a zero-based tuple index, so element 1 is filled.
The marker itself carries or precedes a one-based position, so another element is filled.
witness.observer: The owner submits one value but a different tuple member reaches operations.

open_points.subject: enumeration-valued owner form fields
open_points.question: How does a row identify the particular enumeration whose member value must be read, and which module owns that binding?
options: OwnerFormField carries the enumeration type explicitly
The destination field's declared type determines the enumeration through a specified model-introspection mechanism
Each enumeration-valued destination has a dedicated converter or closed destination entry
open_points.default_guess: Carry the enumeration type explicitly in the row and declare every enum directly named by owner_interface in its models dependency surface.

witness.initial: One form contains a project-erasure kind and another contains a customer transition, both marked FormValueKind.ENUM.
events: owner_interface reads each submitted string.
It must choose the enumeration against which the value is resolved.
outcomes: The row names the correct enumeration and produces the correct member.
The implementation guesses from the destination path or uses one generic enumeration and rejects or misclassifies the value.
witness.observer: The owner sees a valid selection refused or a different action variant performed.

open_points.subject: owner form scalar decoding
open_points.text: as text, as an integer, as true or false, or as an enumeration member's value
open_points.question: What exact input spellings are accepted for integers, booleans and enumeration values, and are matching, signs, leading zeroes, surrounding whitespace and letter case significant?
options: Define strict ASCII canonical spellings for every kind
Use Python's ordinary parsing and enumeration construction
Normalize whitespace and case before parsing
open_points.default_guess: Use strict ASCII integer syntax, exact lowercase `true` and `false`, and exact enumeration values without trimming or case normalization.

witness.initial: A request submits `True` for a boolean field and `01` for an integer field.
events: owner_interface applies the row's FormValueKind conversion.
It builds OwnerRequest or OwnerValues.
outcomes: A permissive decoder accepts both values.
A canonical decoder refuses one or both values.
witness.observer: The owner sees the same form accepted by one implementation and rejected by another.

open_points.subject: failed owner form conversion
open_points.text: A request it cannot read — a body or a head that fails, a form that cannot be decoded — is handed on with no values, nothing partly read kept, and answered by `operations` as any other
open_points.question: Does a field whose text cannot be converted according to FormValueKind make the whole form “cannot be decoded” and discard every value, or is it represented as a field-level invalid value for operations' stage-(4) checks?
options: Discard the entire decoded form and hand operations no values
Preserve all successfully decoded fields and report the failing field as invalid
Refuse in owner_interface without calling operations
open_points.default_guess: Treat conversion failure as whole-form decoding failure and hand operations no values, because the passage explicitly forbids keeping a partial read.

witness.initial: A correction form contains a valid name and a non-integer revision.
events: owner_interface decodes the name successfully and then fails to convert the revision.
The request is handed to operations.
outcomes: operations receives no values and answers failures for missing inputs.
operations receives the name plus an invalid-revision indication and answers a targeted value failure.
witness.observer: The owner sees different failure details and potentially a different first-failing stage.

open_points.subject: OWNER_FORM_FIELDS uniqueness and repeated inputs
open_points.text: A field no row names is not read. The table holds the names so that the page and the reader cannot name a field differently
open_points.question: Must field names be unique in OWNER_FORM_FIELDS, and when a request contains the same named form or query field more than once, which occurrence is read?
options: Require one row per name and refuse repeated request occurrences
Require one row per name and take the first occurrence
Require one row per name and take the last occurrence
Permit multiple rows per name and define fan-out
open_points.default_guess: Require unique table names and reject a request containing repeated occurrences of a scalar field.

witness.initial: A submitted form contains `revision=4&revision=5`, and OWNER_FORM_FIELDS has one revision row.
events: owner_interface looks up the name.
It converts the submitted value to an integer.
outcomes: The first occurrence is used and revision 4 is checked.
The last occurrence is used and revision 5 is checked.
witness.observer: The owner sees the action refused as stale in one implementation and accepted in another.

open_points.subject: special owner-interface fields versus OWNER_FORM_FIELDS
open_points.text:
its target is the query parameter `OWNER_TARGET_PARAMETER` names, its CSRF value the form field `OWNER_CSRF_FIELD` names, every other field it reads or a page writes a row of `OWNER_FORM_FIELDS`

A field no row names is not read.
open_points.question: Are the target and CSRF fields exceptions to “A field no row names is not read,” or must OWNER_FORM_FIELDS also contain rows for them despite the phrase “every other field”?
options: State explicitly that target and CSRF are special fields outside OWNER_FORM_FIELDS
Include target and CSRF rows in OWNER_FORM_FIELDS and remove the “every other” exclusion
Narrow “A field no row names is not read” to ordinary operation-input fields only
open_points.default_guess: Make target and CSRF explicit exceptions outside OWNER_FORM_FIELDS and narrow M29's absolute sentence accordingly.

witness.initial: A valid owner change submits a target parameter, a CSRF field and ordinary operation fields; the table contains only the ordinary fields, as “every other field” directs.
events: owner_interface reads the request.
It applies the M29 statement that a field no row names is not read.
outcomes: The special-case passages prevail: target and CSRF are read outside the table and the request can pass authentication.
The absolute M29 passage prevails: target and CSRF are ignored because no row names them, so the request is refused or has no target.
witness.observer: The owner sees every otherwise valid change accepted or refused.

open_points.subject: OWNER_FORM_FIELDS integrity
open_points.text: The table holds the names so that the page and the reader cannot name a field differently
open_points.question: Which module or release check guarantees that every row has a valid carrier and destination path, that its FormValueKind is compatible with the destination type, that names are unique, and that every ordinary field rendered or read by owner_interface has exactly one row?
options: data_provider validates the table when the release is constructed
owner_interface validates the table at startup
A specified build-time data-closure check validates it
No validation; owner_interface trusts the release table
open_points.default_guess: Assign these coherence checks to the build-time data closure and reject a release with an invalid or incomplete table.

witness.initial: A release row maps a form field to an absent destination path or marks an enum destination as INTEGER.
events: Registry starts and the owner opens and submits the affected page.
owner_interface consumes the row.
outcomes: A release validation rejects the malformed table before Registry can run.
Registry starts, and owner_interface ignores the field, fails at runtime or constructs different values according to its own fallback.
witness.observer: The release operator or owner sees either an admission failure or a runtime form failure.
